newsitem.title: ZAIRE: War unlikely to hit eastern Zaire arabica coffee.
newsitem.headline: War unlikely to hit eastern Zaire arabica coffee.

text.p: The occupation of a swathe of eastern Zaire by rebel fighters is unlikely to affect local production of arabica coffee, although smuggling to Rwanda and Uganda will probably increase, dealers said on Thursday.
"The farms where the coffee is grown are mostly smallholdings and the farmers barely left during the fighting," said one foreign exporter in Goma.
"Coffee is their one means of getting some money and they cannot afford to abandon it even if security is not perfect."

Official figures put exports of arabicas from the region at around 6,000 tonnes in 1995, but dealers say the actual crop may be more than twice that size as a large quantity leaves the country unrecorded.
Arabica-growing areas stretch from Goma through the remote hills of North Kivu along the border with Rwanda and Uganda.
The entire area, as well as a smaller growing area in South Kivu, is now occupied by Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces, which is fighting to topple Zaire president Mobutu Sese Seko.
Although the army was driven out of the region over a month ago, sporadic violence still erupts between the Alliance and village warriors who were their former allies.
"There may be some disruption but it is minimal, particularly compared to what we have seen in Rwanda," said one dealer coming to Zaire from Rwanda for the first time to look for new opportunities.
"Eastern Zaire now has a great deal of potential for an incoming buyer, and the new authorities are beginning to understand what we need."

Officials at the Zairean Coffee Office (OZACAF) said rebel authorities were trying to legitimate export procedures but warned that unless they could provide security for buyers the vast majority of the region's coffee would cross directly into Uganda and Rwanda.
"Unless something is done to reassure buyers then we will be lucky to see a single bean passing through Goma this year," said a senior OZACAF official who would not be named.

The official said that rebel soldiers had seized 200 tonnes of coffee which had been ready for export in December, saying that it was part of the war effort and that the owners would later be compensated.
As a means of bringing badly needed revenue to his new-born administration, Kabila has said coffee growers and exporters should be encouraged.
After vast reserves of gold, which the rebels have yet to effectively exploit, and foreign aid, coffee is the region's biggest foreign exchange earner.
The vast majority of Zaire's coffee crop is robusta, in regions still under the control of Mobutu's army.
